title: Digital Portfolio & Integration Project
subtitle: Everything from this term, gathered, named and captioned. This is the assembly job.
objectives: Explain what a portfolio is and what it is for
Choose which pieces to include and why
Apply the naming and folder rules to real work
Write a caption that says what you would change
Plan a project in stages instead of all at once

cards.title: A portfolio is evidence, not a scrapbook
cards.text: It shows what you can do and how you got there. Everything in it should be there for a reason.

cards.title: The order to build it in
cards.text: Tap through. Gathering and choosing are separate steps on purpose.

cards.title: Do not judge while you collect
cards.text: Collect everything first. Deciding what is good while you are still hunting slows both jobs down.

options: Judging while hunting slows both jobs down
You will forget what you have
question.explain: Two fast passes beat one slow careful one. Gather, then stop, then choose.

cards.title: Three kinds of piece
cards.text: Your best work, your hardest work, and one you improved after feedback. The third one is the most interesting.
points: **Best:** what you can do at your peak.
**Improved:** shows you can take a correction.

cards.title: The draft you fixed is better evidence than the one that was fine
cards.text: Anyone can show a good piece. Showing a bad first attempt and what you did about it is much harder and says more.
points: **That is a portfolio doing its job.**

question.text: A portfolio should include every piece of work from the term.
question.explain: Choosing is the skill. Best, hardest and improved is enough to show what you can do.

cards.title: Halfway
cards.text: Part 2 is naming, captioning and planning the build. Take a break first.

cards.title: Now use everything from week 8
cards.text: Rename every file to the convention, put them in subject folders, and back the whole thing up.

cards.title: Two lines per piece
cards.text: What it was, and what you would change now. The second line is the one a reader actually learns from.
points: **Line two:** what you would do differently.
**'Nothing' is a valid answer** if it is true.

cards.title: This is a build log
cards.text: Players who post a base tour explain why each part is there. That explanation is what makes it worth watching.
points: **Showing the thing** is half of it.
**Explaining the choices** is the other half.
**Without the why**, it is just screenshots.

cards.title: A project is stages, not one big push
cards.text: Break it into named stages with a stopping point in each. A stage you can finish is a stage you will start.
points: **Back up last.** Then it is done.

question.text: What should the second line of a caption say?
question.explain: What it was, then what you would change. The second line is what a reader learns from.

cards.title: A build is photographed at every stage
cards.text: Anyone restoring a car documents the rust before the paint. The before is what makes the after mean anything.
points: **Photograph the mess**, not only the result.

terms.def: A chosen collection of work that shows what you can do.
Choosing what goes in and leaving the rest out.
Two lines: what the piece was, and what you would change.
A part of a project with its own stopping point.
A later version made after feedback.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Stages with stopping points**, then back it up.

teacher.summary: Week 10 is the integration project and it deliberately reuses week 8's naming and folder rules on real work, so the convention is practised rather than memorised. Two ideas carry the lesson. First, gathering and judging are separate passes — a genuinely useful work habit and one that helps a distractible student finish. Second, the improved piece is the most valuable thing in a portfolio, because it is evidence of taking a correction rather than evidence of already being good. The captions are kept to two lines on purpose; longer ones do not get written.
discussion: Ask him which piece from this term he would show first, and why that one.
Ask him to find a piece he improved after feedback, and keep both versions.
Ask what he would change about his best piece, and see whether he can answer without apologising.
Ask him to name the four stages and where he would stop in each.
teacher.extension: Have him actually build it: gather in one sitting, choose and rename in another, caption in a third, back up last. Four short sessions beat one long one that never starts.
misconceptions: 'A portfolio holds everything.' Choosing what to leave out is the skill being assessed.
'Only your best work belongs in it.' The hardest piece and the improved piece say more about you.
'Captions should explain the whole task.' Two lines: what it was, what you would change.
'Do the whole project in one sitting.' Stages with stopping points are what make it startable.
